r.x: Pipe patents

are documents that show when, and in whose name, the idea behind a pipe was registered. Their value to collectors is obvious: a patent number stamped on the shank can fill the gap left by brand catalogs and stamp lists. But the number gives the year an invention was registered, not the year a pipe was made; since a single registered document can remain in use under the same stamp for decades, a patent should be read not as a date on its own but as a lower bound.
Three Documents Often Confused

What the community lumps together as "patents" is actually three distinct document types, each carrying different information for dating purposes. A trademark registration covers the name, letter, or symbol that identifies a product's source; it gives the owner the right to stop others from using a confusingly similar mark, not from making the same kind of goods. So a trademark record tells you which company a stamp belongs to, not how the pipe was made. A design patent protects only a product's outward appearance—the formal features that play no functional role—so because it dates when a family of shapes was registered, it is the most directly useful type for dating. An invention (utility) patent, by contrast, protects a working mechanism; in the US, protection has run for twenty years from the earliest filing date since 1995. A date pulled from a number on a shank, without first distinguishing which of these types it is, is often wrong.
A Gap in the American Records

The US patent system was established by an act of 1790, but the archive's early record is not intact. On December 15, 1836, a fire at Blodgett's Hotel in Washington, which also housed the Patent Office, destroyed roughly ten thousand patent records and thousands of models; only 2,845 records were later reconstructed. Patents granted before the fire are known today by the letter "X"; the sequential numbering system still in use had begun five months before the fire, on July 13, 1836, with document number 1. None of the recovered documents concern pipes. According to the records, the earliest surviving American pipe patent in the archive is dated 1858; the compilation that collector S. Paul Jung Jr. published in 1987 accordingly covers the years 1858 to 1899. The same compilation reports that by the end of the century the annual count of pipe patents had risen to around thirty.
Tying a Stamp to a Document

The records prove most useful for tracing the origin of a known stamp. The Peterson system pipe offers a clear example: the application filed by Dublin's Charles Peterson on September 2, 1891, was granted on May 1, 1894 as number 519,135. The document's own text states that the same invention had already been registered earlier—on August 8, 1890 in Great Britain and Ireland, and on January 22, 1891 in France. This sequence of dates ties the stamps of three countries to a single invention. A similar reading applies to Dunhill patent stamps. Classification makes searching the records easier: in US design registrations, pipes fall under subclass 163 of class D27, titled "Tobacco and Smokers' Supplies." International design applications, meanwhile, use the classification built on WIPO's 1968 Locarno Agreement.
The Limits of the Records

The chief weakness of patent records is that not every registered mechanism was ever manufactured. Nineteenth-century documents are full of inventions—detachable ball-jointed mouthpieces, coiled and serpentine tubes, asbestos-lined chambers, bowls lined with wire mesh, small compartments set aside for nicotine and saliva—most of which are understood never to have reached factory production. Most of the names signed to these documents are not pipe firms at all, but individuals with no means of manufacture. A registration document is therefore proof only that an idea was put on record, not that a briar or meerschaum pipe ever reached the market. In dating, the result stays incomplete unless the document, the catalog, and the stamp are read together.

r.x: The Kaywoodie collector's guide

is a reference text compiled to place American Kaywoodie pipes within the periods mapped out by factory catalogs. The monograph, written by Robert W. Stokes, was originally compiled for Chris Keene's pipe pages before being carried over to Pipedia. The guide does not attempt to give a pipe in hand an exact year; instead, working from factory catalogs dated 1936, 1947, 1955, and 1968-69, plus four undated catalogs, it builds windows along the lines of "present in this catalog, absent from that one."
A Short History of the Brand

The firm's origins trace back to 1851, to a small pipe shop opened in New York's Bowery neighborhood by the German-born Kaufmann brothers. When Bondy joined the partnership in 1854, the name became Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy (KB&B); the clover-leaf stamp inlaid with the KB&B letters was registered in 1881. Sources disagree on when the Kaywoodie name was born: 1915 is commonly cited, though the company's own history states the first Kaywoodie appeared in February 1919. The name is said to derive from a combination of Kaufmann's initial and the English word "wood." In March 1955, S. M. Frank & Co. acquired The Kaywoodie Company along with KB&B and its affiliates; the brand still belongs to that company today.
Reading the Stamp
A collector chasing a date looks at three places: the clover inlaid on the mouthpiece, the shank stamp, and the shape number.

The shape of the leaf gives roughly three phases. On the earliest pipes the clover is elongated and mostly white. The leaf in the 1936 catalog is larger and fuller. At some point between 1936 and 1947, a black clover inside a white circle began appearing on the upper grades while the white leaf continued on the lower grades; the guide cautions that this distinction is not a hard rule, as both leaf types can turn up on pipes of the same grade. A clover rendered only as an outline belongs to a much later period, from the line manufactured in Italy.

The shank stamp helps distinguish marks. Pre-Kaywoodie KB&B pipes and the earliest Kaywoodies carry the KB&B letters inside the leaf; this practice was dropped before 1936. The same leaf also appears on the cheaper Yello-Bole line; the distinguishing mark is the ampersand ("&"), found only on Kaywoodies. The shape number offers a rough threshold too: the earliest pipes used four-digit numbers, reduced to two digits by the 1936 catalog. Records indicate that in the first generation, from 1919 to 1924, these four-digit numbers began with 42.
Quality Grades and Mechanical Hardware

From the 1940s through the 1960s, the line was built on eleven basic grades, starting at the bottom with Drinkless and ending with the Ninety-Fiver and Centennial, thought to have been released for the firm's 95th and 100th anniversaries; the names in between—Super Grain, Relief Grain, and Flame Grain—come from the grain appearance of the briar. This arrangement was not fixed; new grades were added between catalogs, and some were pushed down the ranking.

The number of grades and the number of shapes move in opposite directions. The 1936 catalog lists only four grades, yet presents them across 140 shapes; most of these shapes are simply small, medium, or large versions of the same form, or flat-bottomed variants. By 1947 the grade count rises to twelve while the shape count drops to 69. The 1955 catalog expands the meerschaum side; double-bowl models with a removable inner chamber, and gourd-bodied calabashes, enter the lineup in this period. The same catalog's Chesterfield is Kaywoodie's adaptation of the Peterson system, with a moisture-trapping reservoir built into the shank.

The metal hardware also narrows the window. Drinkless Kaywoodies from 1924-1931 used a push-fit mouthpiece; the screw-in Synchro-Stem was introduced in 1931 and had spread across the whole line by the mid-1930s. A document from those same years provides the paper trail for this hardware: a Canadian patent granted in November 1930 to Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy, based on Rudolph Hirsch's invention, describes an anti-fouling component for a tobacco pipe mouthpiece. The Carburetor introduced in the 1936 catalog was meant to cool the smoke by mixing in air drawn through a hole in the bowl's base; Hirsch's American patent, filed April 21, 1936 and granted June 1, 1937, describes the same principle with an air inlet set into the bowl's base and rising up into the tobacco mass. The filter system changed as well: the Filter-Plus, offered in 1955 with six replaceable screw-in chambers, gave way in the first half of the 1960s to a threaded-base chamber secured with a spring pin.
Limits of the Guide

Stokes does not treat the text as a finished work. Since roughly ten-year gaps separate the catalogs, any innovation that falls between two catalogs can only be inferred from the undated ones; some of the information given for the pre-1936 period is openly speculative. Geography leaves a gap too: the London office opened in 1938 was co-owned with Comoy's of London, and pipes made there do not appear in the American catalogs. For this reason, a date should never be drawn from a single clue—the stamp, the shape number, and the mechanical hardware need to be read together.

r.x: Dating Dunhill before the year code

is the task of placing pipes made before 1921 — the year the brand began striking a small year digit on the shank — into their proper period. In this era, no single mark gives the year; the city line, the patent number, the finish name, and the arrangement of the lettering are read together. The result is often not a single year but a range of two or three. The year 1921, when the use of the year digit began, and the period after it, are covered in a separate entry.
Stages of Production

Alfred Dunhill opened a small tobacconist's shop on Duke Street in the St James's district in 1907. In the early years all the pipes on the counter were commissioned from other workshops; on these examples the shape numbers reportedly stayed between 1 and 30. Starting in 1910, part of production passed into the brand's own hands, but the bowls continued to be turned in France for a long time. It was not until 1920 that the final stage of pipe-making was also brought to London. This is why it is misleading to call a pipe from 1910-1919 simply "English-made": the bowl was shaped in France and the pipe finished in London.

Two markers from the transitional period give further dating help. The white dot on the mouthpiece was first seen as a brand mark in 1912; some compilations place the date at 1915 and explain the dot as a mark showing which face of the mouthpiece should sit on top. Because the two accounts do not agree, the white dot alone is not considered a firm boundary. The sandblasted Shell finish was added in 1917; that same year, briar sourced from Calabria is reported to have come into limited use.
City Line and Letter Arrangement

The most reliable indicator of the period is the branded face of the shank. From 1910 to the autumn of 1918, DUKE ST. S.W. was struck under DUNHILL. In the final months of 1918, LONDON took the bottom line's place, and this layout was kept until 1951; because some sources place the change in November and others at the end of October, the exact day is not certain.

The letter arrangement of the LONDON line also narrows the range. On the very earliest examples, from 1918, the two lines are the same length: the "D" of DUNHILL sits directly above the "L" of LONDON. When the die was re-cut at the end of May 1919, this appearance changed; in the new layout, which began in June, the bottom line spreads to the width of the arc above it, and the "L" and "N" extend past the outer "D" and "L." One warning is in order: records say the 1985 and 2007 anniversary editions reproduced 1910-dated pipes together with their stamp, so not every pipe reading DUKE ST. S.W. is from the early period.
Patent Numbers and Secondary Stamps

The other face of the shank usually carries a patent reference. British patent 5861/12, for the removable inner tube, was applied for in 1912 and granted in 1913; 116989/17, covering the flange that holds the tube in the shank, was applied for in 1917 and published in 1918. On pipes bound for export, the American counterpart of the same invention reads PATENTED MARCH.9.15. Phrases such as "patent applied for" added next to the number narrow the range still further: seen together with 5861/12 it is taken to point to 1917, and together with the American reference, to 1918-1920.

The final layer is finish and quality letters. The "A" in the Bruyere series was struck both circled and bare before 1923, and unstamped without the circle from then on; between June and October 1918 a small round dot was added right after the letter. DR, used on straight-grained bowls from at least 1915, H.W indicating hand-shaping, and LB, which appeared in the war's final months, are the other markers of this period; LB's meaning as "large billiard" rests on a single source. Details of these are gathered in the Dunhill's additional stamps entry.

r.x: The guide to dating Peterson pipes

is a practical rule of thumb aimed not at pinning down an exact year but at placing a pipe within an approximate period. The idea behind it is simple: Ireland's official state name changed several times over the twentieth century, and Peterson updated the origin stamp on its pipes to match each change. The moments when the stamps were renewed thus form a rough calendar.

The reason this guide is called a "rule of thumb" is that the workshop did not immediately pull old stamp dies out of circulation. Because a die forgotten at a bench could resurface years later, it is not unusual to encounter examples that fall outside their period's boundaries. For this reason the stamp is read not on its own, but together with the silver band and the lettering style.
Periods and Origin Stamps

The company's starting point is the small tobacconist's shop Charles Peterson opened in Dublin in 1865; the 1875 partnership with the Kapp brothers produced the name Kapp & Peterson, and the celebrated System pipe was born from that same partnership. In this first period, running from the partnership's founding to the establishment of the Irish Free State in 1922, most pipes carry no origin stamp at all; the habit of stamping only settled in during the First World War, in the block-letter form "Made in Ireland."

Between 1922 and 1937 the "Irish Free State" stamp was used; this stamp is mostly struck close to the mouthpiece end, either parallel or perpendicular to the shank axis. When the country's name changed to Éire under the new constitution that took effect at the end of 1937, the stamp also took on a circular "Made in Eire" form. Because the briar supply broke down during the war years and production was interrupted, exactly how long this stamp lasted is not known with certainty. After the war, circular stamps appear first, followed once again by the block-letter "Made in Ireland." With the declaration of the republic in 1949, the "Made in the Republic of Ireland" stamp begins, and continues to this day.

Peterson's London shop, opened in 1895 and closed at the end of the 1950s, produced a separate family of stamps: inscriptions such as "Made in England," "Made in London," "London England," and "Great Britain" belong to this production.
Silver Band and Lettering Style

On silver-banded examples, the most reliable clue is the three-mark group struck by the Dublin Assay Office: the seated figure of Hibernia denotes the city, the harp the silver standard, and the letter the year. This date is the year the band arrived at the assay office; it may be a year or two before it was actually fitted to a pipe. For the millennium of Dublin's founding, a fourth mark — a shield with three towers — was struck throughout 1988 as well. It is reported that in 1976, under an internationally adopted convention, a separate standard mark consisting of "925" set between the pans of a scale also came into use; examples bearing this mark can only be described as "post-1976."

Lettering style is also distinctive: in the early period the P in "Peterson" has a distinctly forked-tail form, while from the 1930s onward a script-style P and a plain block P are used side by side. Because the old forked-tail letter was revived for commemorative pipes made from the 1970s onward, checking the silver mark is essential on those examples. The clover, fox, and stone-tower symbols seen on some pipes are not standard marks at all but the maker's own stamps; likewise, the "K&P" letters set within a shield are simply the firm's initials.

Series names also give rough help; for example the centenary series dates to 1975, the Mark Twain editions to after 1979, and the Sherlock Holmes series to the late 1980s. The same stamp-reading logic also applies to Dunhill patent stamps; the broader framework of Irish production is gathered in the Irish pipe brands directory.

r.x: Tinned tobacco dating to the 1970s and 1980s

is the subject of a compilation in which John C. Loring gathered the pipe tobacco tins of these two decades into a single table. The piece carries Loring's byline; its Pipedia version carries a contribution from Yang Forcióri. The work does not describe a dating method; it gives a record of tins held in hand, and reads more like a ledger of evidence than a set of method guides.
Layout of the Table

The record has six columns: maker, brand or blend name, tin type, weight, date, and the number of tins matching that description. Over thirty makers are named across more than two hundred rows, and the total of tins counted exceeds six hundred. By row count, the leading headings are, in order, Dunhill, Rattray's, and Balkan Sobranie.

A five-abbreviation key is given for the tin type column. The great majority of rows are CT: a lid twisted open with a coin (coin twist). Second is PT, opened by pulling a ring (pop top). The rest are a handful of rows: LT, a lever-opened lid (lever top), and ST, a canister without an airtight lid, appear only a few times each, while KL, the knife lid defined in the key, does not appear at all. In some rows, the lid color is also added to the CT entry.

A working assumption is stated at the head of the table: unless noted otherwise, the blend is taken to have been made in England. This is why a country is added next to the maker's name; Lane and Drucquer's are marked "USA," Niemeyer "Netherlands," Gallaher's and Murray's "Northern Ireland," Rattray's and Cotton "Scotland." American shop names carrying no country note, by the table's own rule, are taken as English-made; the blends Robert McConnell prepared for Leavitt & Peirce, located at Harvard Square in Massachusetts, appear across four separate rows.
Special Marks in the Date Column

Dates are given at the scale of a decade, but for two brands the abbreviations carry a meaning independent of the calendar. Production of most Dunhill tobacco blends passed in 1981 to Murray, Sons & Co. in Belfast; to separate the tins right at that break, the table uses the abbreviation "L70s" on Dunhill rows. The abbreviation does not mean the late 1970s but points to 1980 and 1981 specifically; that is, it marks not a decade but the last tins made in London. Murray, founded in Belfast in 1810, sold to Carreras in 1953, and later tied through further mergers to the Rothmans group, is also listed in the table under its own name as a maker.

On Rattray's rows, the distinction is by who prepared the blend. "70s" marks tins the Perth shop blended itself, "70s/80s" marks those made after the blends passed to Robert McConnell. The handover is reported to have taken place around 1980, when the shop closed; because some accounts push the change of hands earlier, the year should not be taken as certain. Since the tin label stayed largely the same across both periods, this note is the only thing that separates them.
Patterns in the Table

How the weight is written is itself taken as a period marker. Nearly all tins dated to the '70s carry weight only in ounces (2 oz, 4 oz). On "L70s" rows, the dual form giving grams and ounces side by side (50 gr / 1.76 oz) dominates. Among those dated to the '80s, tins carrying only grams stand out; ounces alone doesn't vanish entirely but recedes. This shift is the concrete counterpart of the weight-unit criterion listed under dating English tinned tobacco.

Brand histories, too, are reflected indirectly in the table. Sobranie, which gave its name to the Balkan blend, is the third-largest heading by row count; although the brand is known to have passed to Gallaher in the early 1980s, the table records the maker throughout as Balkan Sobranie, showing Gallaher only in a separate cluster of rows with its own Northern Ireland blends. There is a single entry from Türkiye: a tobacco listed with the maker Kabataş, carrying the name "Pipo," in a cylindrical tin, dated to the 1950s. No independent production record supporting this row has been found; even so, it can be counted among the rare traces showing that Tekel pipe tobaccos made their way into a collection compiled abroad.
Its Limits

The table is not a census but the inventory of a collection; it shows not how often a given tin was produced but which tins came into the compiler's hands. Although the title names two decades, rows dated to the 1950s and 1960s have also mixed in among them. The dates, too, are not exact years but ranges given based on the tin type, weight notation, and label detail. The compilation should therefore not be taken as evidence on its own; it works as a comparison table to search against once one has a tin in hand.

r.x: Tinned tobacco dating to the 1960s and earlier

is a compilation in which John C. Loring gathered the old tobacco tins in his hands into a single table; its Pipedia version carries a contribution from Yang Forcióri. It is the counterpart to the same compiler's list for the 1970s and 1980s, but looks at a different packaging era: the record begins in the interwar years, when the tin's shape had not yet become standardized.
The Table's Scope

The record has six columns: maker, brand or blend name, tin type, weight, date, and number of tins. One hundred twelve rows name up to thirty-eight makers; a few of these are simply different spellings of the same firm, and the total of tins counted comes to one hundred seventy. Although the dates span the 1930s to the late 1960s, the center of gravity is clear: nearly half the rows carry only the note "50s." Unless stated otherwise, the blend is assumed to have been made in England; entries from Scotland, Ireland, Northern Ireland, Jersey, the Netherlands, Denmark, Japan, Türkiye, and the USA are marked off by a country note next to the maker's name.
Tin Type and Condition Codes

The key at the head of the table defines six abbreviations: CT, a lid twisted open with a coin (coin twist); PT, a lid pulled off by a ring (pop top); LT, a lever-opened lid (lever top); ST, a cylindrical canister; KL, a lid pried off with a knife (knife lid). RUB, meanwhile, is not a tin type but an additional note flagging a rubber gasket exposed on the lid and expected to have degraded.

The distribution is the reverse of that in the later decades. KL is the most common type, at fifty-three rows; CT appears in forty-five rows, three of them carrying the RUB note. ST appears in five rows, LT in three, PT in two. That the later list is dominated by CT and has no KL at all is the clearest sign of the packaging shift between the two eras.

On KL rows, a second mark is added next to the type abbreviation; this mark records not the date but the current condition of the tin, and rests on a single observation: whether the inner lid has bulged outward. Bulged tins are marked "Ex," and the tobacco inside is considered likely to come out intact when opened; tins showing no bulge are marked "OK" and noted as likely to need re-humidifying. "Bd" marks tins suspected that even humidifying would not help. Intermediate grades are given with the suffixes "OK+" and "OK-"; rows with several tins of the same item are written as, for example, "KL-2Ex,1OK." The compilation thus also records what time has done to the tin itself.
Wartime Packaging

Five rows carry "WWII" in the date column instead of a year range. Four of these stand out in terms of packaging: Dunhill's American Mixture appears in a half-pound and one-pound cardboard box, and two blends listed under Peper's appear in glass jars; neither cardboard nor glass appears anywhere else in the list. The fifth wartime entry, Dunhill's blend No. 10, is in the usual knife-lid tin. The withdrawal of tin from civilian packaging during the war years is a well-documented restriction; the decision taken in the US in 1942 is the most commonly cited example. Whether the cardboard and glass containers are connected to this restriction has not been documented, but it fits the dates noted.
What the Maker List Shows

The headings with the most rows are Gallaher's (twelve), Dunhill (ten), BBB and Carroll's (eight each), and Cotton (six). The ranking itself marks an era: while the later list is carried by Dunhill, Rattray's, and Balkan Sobranie, here the weight sits with Belfast, Dundalk, and Edinburgh houses. Gallaher's, founded in Derry in 1857 and later moved to Belfast; Carroll's, which began in 1824 with a tobacconist's shop in Dundalk and is associated with the Mick McQuaid blend; and Edinburgh's Thomson & Porteous, founded, according to records, in 1854 and closed in 1960, represent a generation of names with no counterpart on today's market.

A change of ownership is not always reflected immediately in the label. On the Escudo row the maker is written as Cope's; but Liverpool's Cope Bros had, according to collector records, passed to Gallaher in 1952, while the row's date is the 1960s–1970s. The weight unit also gives a clue: nearly all the entries are in ounces, and of the four rows written in grams, all four date to the 1960s or later; one of the criteria listed in dating English tinned tobacco is thus borne out in this small sample. There is a single row from Türkiye: a tobacco listed with the maker Kabataş, in a 1 3/4-ounce canister, dated to the 1950s. No independent record beyond this table has been found for this name; even so, the row is one of the rare traces showing that pipe tobaccos produced in Türkiye reached collections abroad.

The table's limit follows from this: the record is not a production census but an inventory of the tins that came into the compiler's hands. The dates, too, are not exact years but ranges given based on the tin type, the weight notation, and the label.

r.x: The
Dr. Grabow chronology

is the sequence of events showing how dating is done for a brand where no single stamp gives a year. The brand changed name, address, ownership, and technical fittings over more than a century; the task, with a pipe in hand, is to determine which period's address and which company's name the stamp corresponds to. The brand's general narrative is told in the Dr. Grabow entry, and the course of its model names in the Dr. Grabow series entry.
The Chicago Period

At the head of the chain is M. Linkman & Co., founded in Chicago by Louis B. Linkman in 1892. In 1922 the firm built a three-story factory at the intersection of Fullerton and Racine avenues; because this address appears in advertisements and invoices for decades afterward, it is a concrete clue useful for dating.

The Dr. Grabow name is placed as beginning to be used between 1930 and 1931. The name comes from Paul E. Grabow, a Chicago physician Linkman knew; the details of that relationship are told in the Dr. Grabow legend entry. That the firm began marketing its pipes as "Pre-Smoked" in 1937, and registered both that phrase and the Dr. Grabow name as trademarks in 1947–1948, are links in the chronology traceable at the documentary level.

The Second World War years are the most active period for the stamp. Records say pipe names began to be printed in plain block letters around 1943, the slanted block logo and spade emblem appeared in advertisements toward the end of 1944, and around the same time the firm's name in advertisements took the form "Dr. Grabow Pipe Co." The introduction of two-digit postal-zone numbers in major cities, which was also reflected in address stamps, provides an additional marker.
The Move to North Carolina

The cutting off of Mediterranean briar supply during the war years pushed American makers toward domestic alternatives. In these same years, several American workshops turned to the Appalachian region, where mountain laurel, growing there, was influential as a source of blocks. That Dr. Grabow production moved in 1943 to the town of Sparta in North Carolina appears both in the local press of the time and in the factory's own account; production has continued in the same town since that date.

Linkman's stepping down from the company presidency is placed around 1952; he died in Illinois in January 1957. After this transition, the brand passed into the ownership of Henry Leonard & Thomas, Inc., while production continued at the Sparta facility; the period's directories referring to Dr. Grabow as a product based first in Chicago, then in North Carolina, trace this change of hands. Records say that in 1985 Henry Leonard & Thomas and the Mastercraft line merged with the Sparta-based company under the name Sparta Industries; the brand's transfer to the new company is also placed in the same period.
The Final Links

Sparta Industries merged with Lane Limited in 1997; Lane joined R.J. Reynolds in 1999. In early 2006 the Dr. Grabow line and the Sparta facility were sold to a company called International Pipes & Accessories. Because several months passed between the sale's announcement and the completion of the handover, sources give both January and April as dates.

The function of this sequence in dating a pipe is as follows: a shank bearing the Chicago address points to before 1943, one bearing the Sparta stamp to the later period; the way the company's name is written on the stamp narrows the period further still.

r.x: Dunhill patent stamps

are the marks struck on the shank of a Dunhill pipe that help narrow its production year. On the brand's early pipes, one or two patent numbers sit atop the shank, alongside the brand name and a city line, and from the 1920s onward a small year code as well. Reading these three elements together narrows the production date, in most examples, to a few years, and in favorable cases to a single year.
The Patent Period

What collectors call the "patent period" covers the years during which the habit of stamping a patent number on the shank began and was later dropped; compilations give this range as roughly 1905–1954. Alfred Dunhill's first English patent related to a pipe was filed on 21 November 1904 and granted on 28 September 1905. The document concerns adding a windshield to the bowl, either permanently raised or removable and made of metal or asbestos; the aim was to protect burning tobacco from wind outdoors. Brand history notes that this pipe was developed especially with motorists in mind. Application number 25261 is the basis of the two-line DUNHILL'S over PATENT stamp struck on the shank. These first pipes appeared before Dunhill opened his tobacconist's shop on Duke Street in 1907. It is recounted that the stamp was dropped around 1910, once the brand moved into its own manufacturing and placed DUNHILL over DUKE ST. S.W.; the same records also say the earliest pipes were made of polished Algerian briar and produced in only two shape codes, "T" for billiard and "U" for bulldog.
Inner-Tube Patents

The aluminum inner tube (inner tube) fitted inside the shank is the brand's most prolific source of stamps. English patent 5861/12 was applied for on 8 March 1912 and granted on 6 March 1913; the text describes a removable, straight metal tube with both ends specially shaped. Pipes shipped to America used the American counterpart of the same invention: patent no. 1,130,806, filed 7 March 1913 and granted 9 March 1915, appears on the shank as PATENTED MARCH.9.15 or PAT.AMERICA 1915. English patent 116989/17, in the names of Alfred Dunhill and Thomas George Mandeville, was applied for on 26 September 1917 and published in 1918; its innovation was a flange holding the tube in the shank. From 1918 onward, examples begin appearing where the two numbers sit side by side on the same shank. Another marker of these dates is US patent no. 1,341,418, filed 14 October 1918 and granted 25 May 1920; it describes soaking the wood in oil, heat treatment, and sandblasting to bring out the grain, as a single production sequence.
Brand Stamp and Year Code

When the patent number alone doesn't give a narrow range, the shape of the brand stamp comes into play. The work most often begins from the roughest boundary: since the white dot the brand placed on the mouthpiece began being used in 1912, a pipe with a dot cannot be dated earlier than that. Shank wording shifted to DUNHILL over LONDON at the very end of autumn 1918; because sources give slightly different dates within a few weeks for the transition, the exact day is not certain. Through 1919 the curve and length of the two lines were recut several times, so the alignment of the letters may allow an estimate down to the month. In the same years, the tailed "D" letterform, and whether the "A" stamp is circled or not, is also taken to narrow the range to 1918–1924.

The year-code system was established in 1921. Right after the patent number, sometimes after the word ENGLAND, a small, underlined digit is struck. Compilations report that the digit 1 corresponds to 1921, 0 to 1930, and the numbers 11 through 14 to the years 1931–1934. According to the same records, since the system did not catch on in its first year, a pipe carrying the tailed "D" but no code is generally dated to 1921.
When the Stamp Can't Be Read

It is common for the factory to have skipped striking the code, or for the stamp to have been erased during polishing; in such cases secondary clues are turned to. The MADE IN ENGLAND wording is taken to be found mainly on pipes headed for export up to roughly 1926–1927, and the registration number struck on top of the mouthpiece is taken to have been used from the mid-1910s to the early 1930s. Contradictions between stamps are not unusual; for this reason it is recommended not to rely on a single detail but to look at everything marked on the shank together.

r.x: Comoy's stamp typology

is a method for narrowing the production range of the London firm's pipes by looking not so much at what a stamp says as at how it was struck. The brand never stamped a year code onto a pipe at any point; the date is read not from a single mark but from the combination formed jointly by the letterform, the frame shape, and the mouthpiece mark. The firm's own history is told in the Comoy's of London entry; the general framework of dating is described in the Comoy's dating guide; here the shape of the marks themselves is taken up.
The Shape of the Frame

Two stamps carrying the same words can belong to different periods if their outlines differ. The curving "COMOY'S" and the curving origin wording on the opposite face most often sit not in a full circle but in a squat oval tapering at both ends. A separate group is the mold in which the letters stack to form a closed circle. In the Extraordinaire series, the oval-framed form of the origin wording is seen.

This distinction's boundaries are not sharp. Worn stamp dies were replaced with new ones while the old ones stayed on the bench a while longer; the two forms can therefore turn up side by side on pipes made in the same year. To read the shape number, see the Comoy's shape numbers list.
The Layers of the Origin Wording

The earliest wording is "London Made"; it reaches back as far as 1902, and Comoy's is considered the first London maker to use this phrase. "Made in London," with the word order reversed, is seen on examples stamped 1921, in a straight line beneath the curving brand text. "Made in England" set inside a circle appears on examples dating back to 1910, but only becomes widespread after the 1930s. The circled "Made in London" with a separate "England" line beneath it, on the other hand, is the mark of the postwar export era; no known example predates the Second World War.

The layers don't always line up neatly. On one example whose band shows 1920, two wordings are struck one over the other: a faintly visible "Made in London" with "London Made" struck over it. Such double stampings show that old and new dies were used together during years of transition.
What the Mouthpiece Tells

The inlaid "C" began to be worked into the side face of the mouthpiece around 1919. It is called the "three-piece C" because it requires three separate pieces — one white, two black — and three separate drillings; examples from the 1920s and early 1930s are thinner than postwar ones. On some early pipes the letter sits not on the side face but on top of the mouthpiece. The practice was dropped in the early 1980s, in the Cadogan period; it was replaced first by a single-hole inlay with the letter at its center, then by laser printing. Along with the mouthpiece material, this detail also gives away a mouthpiece that has since been replaced. In the Grand Slam series, meanwhile, a white-turquoise-white striped bar logo was used between 1933 and 1945; after the war this series too returned to the three-piece "C."
Examples Anchored to the Calendar

The typology above is pinned to the calendar thanks to pipes whose year letter can be read. If the band between the shank and mouthpiece is silver, three marks are looked for on it: the walking lion showing the fineness, the symbol showing the assay office (a leopard's head for London), and the letter giving the year. The year-letter system in England goes back to 1478 and changes every year. Even so, the result isn't absolute: since bands arrived at the factory in batches, they may have been fitted months, even a year, after being struck; a band may also have been added much later to repair a cracked shank.

r.x: The
Dating Guide Addendum

is a correction note added after the fact to the established guides used for dating Dunhill pipes. Its subject is narrow but its consequence is directly practical: the number and validity range of two patents registered in Canada turn out to differ from what the guides had said. The correction rests not on interpretation but on documents; the summary records in the online patent database of the Canadian Intellectual Property Office redraw the range a stamp can point to. For the general role of patent stamps in dating, see the entry on pipe patents.
The Vernon Joint and Registration No. 325.090

The Vernon joint is a threaded tenon mechanism used where the mouthpiece meets the shank; records say it was introduced in 1931 and is seen up to the Second World War. Its Canadian registration has at times been given in guides as 356.090, but the number in the official record is
; the discrepancy is explained as a typographical error arising from transposed digits. The record defines the patent under the heading "mouthpiece for tobacco pipes and the like."
The real correction is in the date. While the guides had assumed the registration dated to the mid-1930s, the CIPO record gives the grant date as
16 August 1932

, and the end of the protection period as 16 August 1949. Under Canadian practice of the period, protection ran seventeen years from grant, so the two dates confirm each other. For a collector, the result is concrete: a pipe carrying this stamp can be dated a few years earlier than the guides had indicated. The upper bound, on the other hand, is not equally reliable; there is no evidence that production continued through to the end of the protection period, so 1949 is not a closing year but, at best, an upper frame.
The Flanged Inner Tube and Registration No. 197.365

The second correction concerns the flanged inner tube fitted inside the shank. The guides place this stamp in the range 1927–1941. The CIPO record, however, points to a different table: registration no. 197.365 was granted on
17 February 1920

and lapsed with the end of its seventeen years on 17 February 1937. The record's title is a general phrase, "tobacco pipe and cigar holder," so the information tying the number directly to the flanged inner tube comes from guide tradition. Set side by side, the two ranges produce a considerable shift in the earliest and latest years the stamp could be expected to appear.

The reason for the shift is not clear. The common explanation is that the older Canadian registration no. 158.709, for the unflanged inner tube, remained in force for a time and delayed use of the new stamp; but the year that registration expired is not consistent across sources, and the explanation isn't strong enough to carry the weight on its own. Nor is it seen as unusual for more than one registration to be used side by side in the same years: on the British side, registrations 5861/12 and 116989/17 are reported to have been used together for a period. In this case, the most measured conclusion is that the stamp may be seen within the protection period, that is between 1920 and 1937, on pipes headed for the Canadian market.
The Correction's Value for Dating

These two notes do not replace a guide on their own; they are footnotes added to the margins of the existing guides. The lesson they carry, though, is general: a patent stamp shows not the year of manufacture but the range during which the registration was valid, and that range can only be tested against the official record. For a comprehensive reading of Dunhill stamps, the Dunhill patent stamps and Dunhill dating entries should be read together. As new examples surface, these ranges can be expected to narrow further still.

r.x: The mystery of the White Spot

is the question of why the small white dot on the stem of a Dunhill pipe became so recognisable. The answer is less ornate than one might expect: the dot was born not as an emblem but as a practical convenience, and only later turned into the brand's signature. Today that same mark serves as the starting point for a production record spanning more than a century.
Origin of the Spot

Alfred Dunhill's shop on Duke Street in London opened in 1907; in the early years pipes were commissioned from outside makers, and control of production gradually passed into the brand's own hands. The hard rubber (vulcanite) mouthpieces shaped by hand were made so symmetrically that customers had trouble telling which face of the mouthpiece was meant to sit on top. According to most records, a white dot was placed on the upper face of the mouthpiece to solve this problem in 1915; some compilations put the date at 1912. The mark's purpose was to indicate orientation, but it quickly became the brand's most visible distinguishing feature.
A Record System That Makes the Collection Legible

Dunhill's weight among collectors does not come from craftsmanship alone. Unlike most makers, Dunhill, from an early date, struck shanks with stamps that left a trace of the year one by one. Patent numbers, the small year digit added next to the ENGLAND lettering, and finish names, read together, often place a pipe in a single year. The details of these methods are covered in the Dunhill dating guide. The most frequently cited example in stamp charts is number 417574: records say the bare form of the number points to the second half of the 1930s, while the version with "/34" appended points to the 1940s and 1950s. Most of these numbers are the registration traces of devices peculiar to Dunhill, such as the inner tube fitted into the shank and its sandblasting.

On early examples the meaning of the stamp was also different. Records say that on 1910s pipes, the number struck on the shank did not indicate the shape but the size of the inner tube used; the same pipe later acquired a lettered shape name in subsequent catalogues. It took years for the shape-number system to settle in, and today it is tracked with its own separate shape list.
Finishes and Shapes

The distinction that stands out most in a Dunhill collection is the finish. The smooth-polished Bruyere ranks as the oldest; the first of the sandblasts, Shell, was added in 1917. Root, which brings out the grain, was introduced around 1930-1931, the light-brown sandblast Tanshell in 1952, and the reddish Redbark in 1972; sources report a one-year slip on some of these dates. The dark-brown Cumberland is placed around 1979-1980. Lining up the same shape across different finishes is the most common way collections are arranged.

On the shape side, the frequently encountered examples include the long-shanked Lovat, straight and bent bulldog variants, army-mounted princes, and short models sized to fit a waistcoat pocket. On some of these, the patent number struck onto the silver band remains the sole dating clue where there is no year digit on the shank. Later-fitted bands, repair traces, and re-struck grade stamps also occur; this is why it is standard practice to look at all the stamps together rather than at any single mark.

r.x: Dunhill's shape repertoire

isn't limited to the numbered standard list. In the brand's catalogues and stamps are shapes that never entered the list at all, or appeared for only a few years before disappearing. Among these, the trio that has occupied collectors most is Don, Duke, and Opera; all three look familiar at first glance, but each follows its own rules in the details.
The Fine Line Between Don and Duke

Both shapes are relatives of the poker family: a cylindrical bowl, a flat-sitting base. The distinction knots at the shank. The Don has a real shank, short as it may be, and the mouthpiece sits on it. The Duke has no shank at all: a metal band set into the side face of the bowl does the shank's job, and the mouthpiece attaches directly into that socket. The Duke's mouthpiece is most often two pieces: a thin body with a flared bit at the end; the body is made in some examples of ebonite (vulcanite), in others of bone. This construction lightens the pipe noticeably.

The Duke's bowl leans slightly forward and balances on a flattened heel; the mouthpiece sits right below the bowl's waistline. Records show the shape stamped with the numbers 519, 4144, and 41441, and produced in the Bruyere, Shell, Tanshell, Red Bark, and Root Briar finishes. Its production is said to have begun in the mid-1910s and continued intermittently to the present day. A similar bowl-and-band arrangement turns up under different names at other makers; some shape charts note that Peterson calls the same construction tankard. The entry on the origin of briar pipe shape names gives detail on how shape names shift from one brand to another.
Opera and Quaint Records

The Opera is a small pipe with an oval bowl flattened from the sides. The flat cross-section is no accident: the pipe is sized this way so it won't bulge in the narrow pocket of evening dress; its name, too, comes from the setting where this carrying habit prevailed. According to information passed down from Dunhill's own product management, the shape's trail can be traced back to the fourth edition of the 1922 catalogue
About Smoke

, which featured three separate flat-bowled Quaint shapes. Records say two of these were straight and one bent, coded in the period's system as FS, FB, and FC respectively. FB was a flat-bodied bulldog; for the classic version of this family, see the entry on the Bulldog and Rhodesian.

In the Dunhill vocabulary, the word Quaint does not name a single shape but covers the entirety of shapes that don't fit the standard shape chart. When the particular structure of a briar block took the maker outside the chart's measures, the resulting pipes were gathered under this heading. The Vest Pocket, from the same family, offers an even flatter silhouette with its oval bowl and a mouthpiece attached at a near-vertical angle.
Why They Get Confused

These three shapes form a closely related cluster along with the Poker, Cherrywood, and Friendly. The place to look for the distinction is always the same: is there a shank, does the band serve as the carrier, is the bowl's cross-section round or oval. The number on the stamp is also a guide; for a rundown of the numbers, see Dunhill shape numbers, and for reading the stamps' years, see Dunhill dating.

r.x: Dating a Loewe pipe

is not a matter of reading a year off a stamp, but of layering several clues to narrow things down to a range. The firm never, at any point, struck a mark that directly gave the production year. What remains are the layout of the shank stamps, whether or not a series name is present, the switch on the underside from a shape name to a three-digit number, and, on silver-banded examples, the assay mark. The brand's general history is covered in the Loewe & Co. entry.
Stamp Layout

The classic arrangement is spread across three surfaces: on the left side, "L&Co." within an oval frame; on the right side, "Loewe London W."; and on the underside, the shape name. On pipes destined for export in particular, a circled "Made in England" mark is also added to the underside. This layout stayed remarkably unchanged for decades, which is precisely what makes dating so difficult.

The distinguishing layer is the second line on the left side. On early pipes, the space beneath the oval logo is blank; the firm had not yet adopted a named quality grade in those years. With the addition of the names Centurion, Original, and Old English, a two-line stamp forms on the left side. Accounts differ on the year these names were introduced: one account gives 1955, while another, based on stamp archives, gives 1956 to 1964. Where the two sources agree is that pipes dated before 1920 carry no series stamp at all. The names Standard, Spigot, and Mounted were added to the list later; a pipe bearing one of these names dates from the later period.

The upper grades fall outside this layout. The Extra Grain, Straight Grain, and Special Grain stamps take the place of the shape name on the underside; below them only the circled origin mark remains. According to one account these three names rank in that order from top to bottom, but because these grades were produced in very small numbers, the ranking has not been confirmed by independent records.
From Shape Name to Number

The most useful break comes from the removal of the shape name on the underside. Loewe long referred to its shapes not by number but by names specific to the English shape catalogue; at some point these were replaced by three-digit numbers beginning with nine. The most classic form, the billiard, for example, carries the number 910. Sources place the year of the transition anywhere between 1960 and 1967, and it is also reported that the two systems ran side by side for a while. Since the numbered system continued through the following period, a pipe bearing a three-digit number is considered late; one bearing a shape name is placed in the earlier period. As with the dating of Comoy's, it is not a single clue but the intersection of clues that yields a result here.
Silver Band and Assay Mark

The most reliable evidence is silver. In the English system, the walking lion indicates sterling standard, the leopard's head the London assay office, and the letter the year the mark was struck; the year letter was a mandatory component until 1999. Because Loewe's spigot mount, which also has its own series name, made silver-banded examples relatively common, this method works better here than it does for many contemporaries. It is reported that in the later period, the workshop that carried out the group's silverwork kept sending bands to the assay office, so even the newest pipes can be dated from the stamp.
Confusing Details

Because the stamp dies stayed the same when ownership changed hands, it is not possible to sort a pipe into periods from the lettering alone. Even the year of the takeover is inconsistent across sources: one account says Civic bought the firm in 1920, while the real break that changed the character of production came around 1964; other records simply say "before 1960." The Cadogan period, when the brand was grouped under the same roof as GBD and Comoy's, is somewhat clearer; the transfer of the trademark into this group is cited as 1979. Pipes from this period bearing the circled origin stamp in the Comoy's pattern is considered a practical way of recognising late examples. The brand also has second-quality names: the two-digit shape-numbered Haymarket is cited for the early period, and the Beefeater stamp for later years. Pipes bearing these stamps are treated not as Loewe proper but as a second-quality line.

r.x: Dating Charatan pipes

proceeds indirectly, since the Charatan brand never used a year code: a pipe is placed in a period by looking at the traces successive changes of ownership left on the shank and mouthpiece. These traces alone do not give a single year, but stacked together they let most pipes settle into a range of a few years. The method's one requirement is that the mouthpiece be original; a later-fitted mouthpiece removes one of the two most decisive clues at once, leaving only the shank wording.
Shank Wording and Shape Code

The number of lines struck on the shank is the most practical starting point for placing a period. Up to the 1960s, "CHARATAN'S MAKE LONDON ENGLAND" reads in two lines, and the shape code consists only of digits. Letters added to that code mark the following period: a DC suffix shows the pipe left the factory with a Double Comfort mouthpiece, an X suffix shows it left with a saddle mouthpiece without Double Comfort. If either of these letters is in the code, the pipe dates to after 1960.

The "MADE BY HAND" stamp is reported to have first been struck in 1958, though some records push this a few years earlier or later. In the mid-1960s this wording moved to a three-line arrangement, and shortly after changed from block capitals to a script character. The £ sign seen inside a circle on the shank, the Lane stamp, is not on its own proof of ownership; records say this same stamp was also struck on pipes shipped in years when Lane was still only the American importer. Once production moved to France, wording foregrounding London disappears and is replaced by "CHARATAN of London"; some examples also show a "France" mark on the shank or mouthpiece.
Mouthpiece Shape and the CP Emblem

The second measure confirming the shape-code suffix is the mouthpiece itself. Early pipes used ordinary tapered or saddle mouthpieces; the Double Comfort mouthpiece, with its two-step bite section, was an innovation of the Lane management and has continued to the present. Accordingly, a pipe with a tapered mouthpiece is taken as pre-Lane, one with a Double Comfort mouthpiece as post-1960. Since the saddle mouthpiece appears in both periods, the decision in that case is left to the X suffix in the shape code.

The interlocking CP emblem struck on the mouthpiece also falls roughly into four phases. In the oldest stamps the letters are worked thinly and the C sits inside the P; in the Lane years this same arrangement thickens noticeably. Reportedly, from around 1980 onward, the C no longer sits inside the P; the two letters simply stand joined side by side. The emblems of the Dunhill and Russell periods also differ from each other, though this distinction is only noticeable through comparative study.
Periods and Uncertainties

The division established among enthusiasts follows the firm's ownership history: founder Frederick Charatan's initial period, begun in London in 1863; his son Reuben's period from 1910; then the Lane Limited years; the Dunhill years; the J. B. Russell period; and a second Dunhill period beginning around 2000. The Dunhill years split into two on their own: the early years when production continued at the old London factory, and the later years after that factory closed in 1982 and the work was transferred to the Parker-Hardcastle facility in Walthamstow. In the Russell period, production moved to France, to the town of Saint-Claude, and after 2000 continued at the Invicta Briars workshop run by Colin Fromm.

The boundaries of this framework shift from source to source. For Reuben's death and the firm's sale, the years 1960, 1962, and 1963 are all given; Dunhill's takeover is variously placed at mid-1976 or 1978; the end of the Russell period varies between 2000 and 2002. For this reason, pipes falling close to a period boundary should be given a margin of a few years' uncertainty.

r.x: The Dunhill White Spot Guarantee

is the name given to the replacement pledge associated with the white dot on the stem of Dunhill pipes. Its importance for dating lies less in the guarantee itself than in what it produced: defining a renewal period required a mark that could document when a pipe had gone on sale, and that need opened the path to the year-code system collectors rely on today.
The Need Behind the Stamp

For a brand to set a limit such as "within twelve months," it needs a way to show when that period began. In the counter of a single London shop, this information could live in the seller's memory; it could not in independent distributors scattered around the world. Dunhill began stamping pipes with a numeric year code in 1922, and also marked pipes replaced under the guarantee with an additional "EX" stamp. Together, these two marks made it possible to police both the time limit and the rule that a replaced pipe would not be replaced again.

Pipes made before 1922 carry no year code; dating them instead relies on changes in the form of the "DUNHILL" and "LONDON" lettering — a dotted or dotless "A," an arched arrangement, the length ratio between the two words, the tail of the "D." For a breakdown of these details, see the entries on Dunhill Patent Stamps and Dating and Dunhill's Additional Stamps.
The Evolution of the Guarantee Text

In its first About Smoke catalog, published in 1910 when the firm entered briar pipe production, it promised a replacement for a defective pipe with no time limit stated; the same wording appears in the 1917 catalog as well. The exact year the white dot appeared on the stem is not certain: sources give dates ranging between 1912 and 1915, and most accounts hold that the dot's original purpose was to show which side of the stem faced up on a straight pipe.

The shift from an unlimited pledge to a time-limited one falls in the postwar years. According to reports, the name "White Spot" first appears in a 1919 price supplement, though without stated conditions; a catalog from around 1920 limits the renewal right to twelve months, and the following year's edition adds that a pipe replaced under guarantee will not be replaced again. The dates for these two steps rest on a single study and have not been independently confirmed against catalog records. By contrast, the 1921 catalog text and the 1922 introduction of the year code and EX marking appear the same way across Dunhill dating guides as well.

Later narrowings of the guarantee likewise rest on single sources: the 1923 catalog is said to have limited free replacement to cases of a cracked or burned bowl, with other repairs charged for, while some American advertising copy from the mid-1920s reportedly shortened the period to ninety days. The 1928 French-language catalog is said to simplify the wording again, stating that a pipe with a manufacturing defect within one year would be replaced free of charge, once only.

For collectors, the practical takeaway of this chronology is simple: a Dunhill without a year code belongs either to the period before the guarantee became time-limited, or to the transitional years, and dating it falls back on the form of the stamps. These details are best weighed together with the criteria discussed in the entry The Mystery of the White Spot.

r.x: Dating Castello pipes

relies not on a single year code but on several successive generations of stamps. The workshop was founded in 1947 by Carlo Scotti in Cantù; the wording, letters, and symbols used since then are usually enough to place a pipe within a decade, and after 1987 directly within its year. The following criteria require reading the stamps together: none gives a certain result on its own.
Early Wording

In the years right after founding, pipes were stamped "Mi Reserva," roughly "my own reserve"; records take this wording to mark production between 1947 and 1950. In the following period, "Reg No" was added to the stamp. This number is often mistaken for a shape number; in fact it is only the company's trademark registration number and has nothing to do with the pipe's shape.

The shape number itself does not give a date on its own, but it needs to be read. A digit placed before the number indicates the nature of the shape: a 2 means the bowl has been treated in an ornate variation; a 3 means the carving is out of the ordinary. Reportedly, numbers beginning with 3 were in time replaced by the symbol π; the year this change was made is not documented.

The mark on the mouthpiece is also distinguishing. The first symbol used was the white bar. Castello beginning to work with American distributor Wally Frank changed this: since the distributor's own product line already carried the name "White Bar," a diamond-look stone inlay was designed for the American market. On white acrylic mouthpieces, a black dot is used instead.
Size and Quality Letters

The first form of the letter system indicated only size. Reportedly, on pipes falling between the late 1950s and the mid-1960s, the letters SA, SB, SC, and SS were used, SA the smallest measure and SS the largest. Because this range rests on a single compilation, it should not be taken as a firm boundary.

Franco "Kino" Coppo joined the business in 1969; the grading based on the large letter "K" also became established around the late 1960s and early 1970s. On sandblast and carved surfaces this letter conveys only size; on smooth surfaces it conveys the nature of the grain together with the size. These same years are the years the workshop moved fully from hand-finished machine production to entirely handmade production.

In 1982 the large "K" was dropped for the lowercase "k": a single letter is given inside a circle, two or more inside an oval. This distinction is the most practical way to divide a pipe into pre- and post-1982.
The Castle Stamp and Additional Marks

In 1987, on the brand's fortieth year, a castle stamp containing a number began to be used. Adding the number to 1947 gives the manufacture year; a pipe with "50" in the castle is a 1997 piece. The stamp is not found on every pipe, so its absence alone is not taken as a dating indicator.

The codes give no date; they are useful only for understanding which market a pipe was prepared for. For the general framework of stamp reading, see pipe stamps and logos, and for the brand's own history, see Castello.

Management of the firm had passed, from the early 1980s, to Carlo Scotti's daughter Savina and her husband Franco Coppo; Scotti died in 1992. This continuity, which Coppo maintained until his death in 2025, also helped preserve the stamp system largely intact. The workshop's management today rests with Coppo's daughter Stefania Coppo.

r.x: Rudolfs Patent

is less a brand than a stamp. No documents survive tying it to a firm, a founder, or a registration beyond the handful of pipes that carry it, so this entry is limited to what those surviving examples themselves show. Collectors discuss the stamp mainly because its layout and mouthpiece design closely echo a far better-known maker of the period, Peterson.
Appearance of the Stamp

The name is struck across the shank in an arched curve, with the word PATENT set directly beneath it at the center of that arc. The drawing of the initial R is closely related to the shape of the P in Peterson stamps. Taken together, the placement, letter proportions, and word order clearly follow an established pattern of the period. One known example also carries PRIMA beneath the name. PRIMA is a grade stamp also used on Comoy's of London pipes, but Comoy's dating guides place that stamp in the second half of the 1910s, so no overlapping period has been established between the two marks. Their appearing together on the same pipe may point to an exchange of stems or stamps among English workshops, but on its own it proves no production link.
Dating

The only solid basis for a date is a silver band. One known example's band carries the anchor city mark of the Birmingham Assay Office along with the letter that corresponds to 1909 in that office's annual letter cycle. Because the year letter in English hallmarking changes every year, this pins the year the silver was hallmarked to within a single year. Only one pipe is known to offer this evidence, however, so 1909 marks the age of that particular example rather than the whole period during which the stamp was used. Examples lacking a stamp or a band offer no such basis, leaving only a rough estimate from the form of the stamp itself. For the general place of hallmarks in dating, see the entry on pipe patents and registration records.
The Mouthpiece and the Patent Question

The word "patent" in the name is thought most likely to refer to the mouthpiece, since that is where the genuinely original element lies. The tip of the mouthpiece resembles Peterson's P-lip shape: a flattened tip that directs smoke toward the roof of the mouth. Here, however, instead of Peterson's single hole there is a broader flat surface with two separate draft channels. A similar tip design appears on the system pipes made by BBB under the name Glokar; the Glokar patent is reported to have been taken out in 1905, though that date has not been confirmed by any independent registration record. The order in which these three designs emerged, and which registrations they rested on, has never been documented. The patent number, filing date, and rights holder behind the Rudolfs stamp remain unknown today, and the entry should be read with that gap in mind until a new document or catalogue page comes to light.

r.x: Pipe stamps and logos

are the whole of the written and visual marks a maker leaves on a pipe. On a pipe whose box, receipt, and catalog have long since vanished, these marks are often the only surviving record. The letters struck into the side of the shank give the brand, country, quality grade, and shape number; the inlay or stamped mark set into the stem is the visual signature that identifies the brand from a distance. Read together, the two yield both an identity and an approximate production window.
The Layers on the Shank

A shank stamp is not a single piece of information but several layered together. The most stable element is the brand name; alongside it, most makers include a country-of-origin mark, a quality name, and a shape number. Quality names vary from brand to brand: some firms use a number, some a letter, and some strike the series name directly. A shape number, meanwhile, only makes sense against that particular brand's own shape chart; the same digit can correspond to an entirely different shape at two different firms.

The country-of-origin mark is especially valuable for dating. In the United States, the McKinley Tariff Act of 1890 required, starting March 1, 1891, that imported goods carry the country of origin marked legibly; at the time, the country name alone was enough. According to accounts, the explicit requirement for the "Made in" phrasing became established only in the first quarter of the twentieth century, through later customs regulations. This is why a pipe marked only "England" on the shank and one marked "Made in England" can point to different periods even though they look alike. The framing, line arrangement, and lettering style of the mark also distinguish periods; for a detailed example, see the entry on Comoy's stamp typology.
The Mark on the Stem

The logo set into the stem is the brand's most easily recognized face. Some firms use a single dot, some a specific series of dots, and some a letter-shaped inlay. The material, size, and number of pieces making up the inlay all changed over time, so these details also help narrow down a period. On brands like Dunhill and Sasieni, the stem mark has become almost as recognizable as the brand name itself. Because the stem is a replaceable part, a logo that conflicts with the shank stamp should always be questioned.
Verification and Its Limits

The main comparative source for these marks is the pipephil.eu database, which photographically documents shank and stem stamps and covers thousands of brands. The site indexes brands by letter, dot, geometric shape, and symbol groups, and can also be browsed by country.

Even so, a stamp alone rarely gives a definitive answer. When worn dies were replaced with new ones, old and new forms were sometimes used side by side for a while, producing faint or double-struck stamps. Polishing can wear away part of a stamp entirely. For this reason, marks are best weighed alongside other evidence wherever possible: the year letter on the silver band between shank and stem, any patent number, and the period style of the briar work on the pipe's body together give a far more reliable result.

r.x: A Dunhill ES at auction

is a small case often cited to illustrate how far stamp reading can take a collector. John C. Loring examined a pipe listed at an online auction using nothing but the listing text and the photographs, and found a mismatch between what the shank writing claimed and what the bowl actually showed. According to the listing, the pipe was a 1923 ES, the long-shanked Canadian shape in the brand's lineup.
The Listing's Claim

The single marker that tied the listing to 1923 was a small digit — a half-height, underlined 3 — struck right after the inner-tube patent number. In the Dunhill stamp layout, this small digit is a year code, and 3 corresponds to 1923. The same face of the shank also carried the MADE IN ENGLAND inscription and the ES shape code, while the other face carried the DUNHILL-over-LONDON line and the H.W. handwork stamp. The seller described the bowl as a Bruyere billiard with an oval-section shank, gave measurements of roughly fifteen centimetres in length and about four and a half centimetres in bowl height, and noted that the stamps had faded from repeated polishing and that the metal inner tube was missing.
Where the Photos Disagreed

The first thing that stood out in the images was the proportions. An ES shape is expected to have a shank noticeably longer than the mouthpiece, yet on this pipe the mouthpiece was longer than the shank. Since the code is generally taken to stand for "extended shank," this reversal of proportion undercuts the very feature that defines the shape. The second detail was the position of the writing: instead of being centred, the shank text had shifted down toward the mouthpiece end, and the letters gave the impression of having been struck one at a time rather than from a single two-line block stamp. Third, the DUNHILL and LONDON lines appeared almost equal in length; this style points not to the period after the year-code system was set up, but to the last months of 1918.
The Repair Hypothesis

Loring places these three observations in the framework of the brand's early repair practices. It is reported that when the factory repaired a pipe, it stamped the year of the repair, reproduced the original stamps as closely as it could, and — because the dies from the 1910s were no longer on hand a decade later — often redid this re-stamping letter by letter. From this, the explanation follows: the pipe may in fact be a 1918 ES. Its shank likely broke, it returned to the factory in 1923, the broken section was cut off and discarded, the lost length was made up with a longer mouthpiece, and the shank writing was renewed letter by letter. The shortening of the shank, on its own, explains both the reversed proportion and the writing's apparently shifted-down position.
The Lesson the Case Leaves Behind

Loring himself notes that this conclusion rests on photographs alone and therefore carries probability, not certainty. The real value of the method lies elsewhere: a year code can tell you not when a pipe was made, but when the shank was last stamped. Secondary markers such as mouthpiece authenticity, the diameter of the white spot, or the shape of the letters only carry meaning together, never on their own. A repair does not erase a pipe's date within the Dunhill system — but it does open up the question of whether the pipe still deserves the shape name it carries.

r.x: The
Comoy's dating guide

gathers the ways of placing the London firm Comoy's pipes into a production range based on their stamps. The firm never at any point struck a mark giving the production year directly on a pipe; since there is no year code to check as with Dunhill pipes, the date is narrowed by stacking together the shape of the brand wording, the origin stamp, the "C" inlaid on the mouthpiece, and the series name. The result is most often not a single year but a range of several years. The firm's general history is told in the Comoy's of London entry.
Period Lines

The family, according to records, began pipe making with François Comoy in the French town of Saint-Claude in 1825; briar (funda kökü) became the main material in these workshops a short time later. Henri Comoy, born in 1850, moved to London in 1879 and opened a small workshop in Seven Dials. Production moved to Clerkenwell in 1895 and to a larger building in 1913; the business was incorporated in 1914 as H. Comoy & Co. Ltd. Henri died in 1924 at seventy-four, and the firm passed to his nephews Louis and Charles Chapuis. Records say the firm came under the umbrella of Cadogan Investments Ltd. in 1929, which brought together the pipe companies of Civic and Oppenheimer. Because production shrank to a small workshop during the Second World War, Comoy's pipes from the 1940s are scarce. Family control passed entirely to Cadogan in the early 1980s; this date marks the main dividing line in the collection.
Brand and Origin Stamps

On the earliest pipes "Comoy's" is struck in forward-leaning, joined script, carrying a long tail running back from beneath the "s." This form points to roughly 1900–1919. From around 1917 to the late 1930s, the stamp turns to a curving capital letterform: serif letters, an apostrophe, and a "C" larger than the rest. This curving stamp was also used briefly right after the war. Around 1945 the wording drops to a straight line. After the 1950s the stamp moves to block letters; three variants are distinguished: an unserifed form with an apostrophe and a large "C," a serifed form with the same features, and a short-lived form with no apostrophe and a shrunken "C." Because new dies were ordered as old ones wore out, old and new molds were used side by side for a while, blurring the years of transition.

The origin stamp adds a separate layer. "London Made," in one line or two, reaches back as far as 1902; when it was dropped is debated, with stamp archives giving the mid-1910s and part of the pipe literature giving the 1930s. Comoy's is considered the first London maker to use this wording. "Made in England" is set inside a circle; examples dating back to 1910 are known, but it becomes truly widespread only in the 1930s. The circled "Made in London" with a straight "England" line right beneath it, on the other hand, emerges with the postwar export push, in the early 1950s.
The Three-Piece "C" on the Mouthpiece

The brand's inlaid "C" symbol began to be worked into the side face of the mouthpiece around 1919. The letter is not a single piece: the center of a round white inlay and the open mouth of the letter are drilled separately and filled with shrinking black pieces. Because it requires three separate drillings, this workmanship is known as the "three-piece C" and continues into the Cadogan period. Examples from the 1920s and early 1930s are noticeably thinner than postwar ones. Cadogan moved first to a single-hole inlay with a "C" at its center, then to laser printing.
Series Names and the Silver Band

Series names also narrow the range. Prima was the top grade in the early 1900s; Tradition was released in 1925 for the firm's hundredth year. Grand Slam, together with a metal filter mechanism set into the shank, was introduced in 1933; the US patent no. 2,001,612 read on these pipes was filed that same year and granted in 1935. The name Blue Riband comes from the title given to the fastest ocean liner crossing the Atlantic; Cunard's Queen Mary took this record in August 1936. London Pride sat just below, a step with a lighter finish. Old Bruyere and Virgin Briar, meanwhile, no longer appear in the 1965 catalogue; these names point to an earlier period.

The most decisive anchor is the mark on the silver band. In the English system, the walking lion shows the fineness of the silver, the leopard's head the London assay office, and the letter the year; the year-letter practice goes back to 1478. Because bands arrived at the factory in batches, the year the mark gives can be a year earlier than the pipe itself; even so, no other clue gives as narrow a range as this one.
