r.x: Sasieni's subsidiary brands

are the secondary pipe lines the London firm Sasieni sold under separate names beneath its flagship series, Four Dot. There is no mark on these pipes that gives the production year directly; dating relies on reading together the distributor name that appears in catalogues and advertisements, the layout of the shank stamp, the shape number, and the finish name. For the firm's general history, see the Sasieni entry.
The Origin of the Lines

Sasieni's founding rested on a patent for oven-curing briar bowls; the application was filed on 6 January 1919 and the text published that same March. The device, which described briar bowls fitted to rotating panels in a heated chamber and periodically removed to have surface moisture wiped off, compressed the years of natural drying into weeks. In the founder's 1924 US patent, his address is given as the Stoke Newington district of London; patents taken out in the same years cover an extension that keeps moisture from reaching the joint between mouthpiece and bowl. This early cluster of patents is considered the main factor that let him leave the Dunhill workshop and begin producing under his own name.

The grading standard was strict; as bowls that failed to earn the Four Dot stamp but whose flaws stayed on the surface piled up, separate lines were opened to make use of them. In the 1935-1937 catalogues of the American distributor London House, eight names are listed: His Royal Highness, Royal Stuart, Friar, Mayfair, Henley Club, Pickwick (later Mr. Pickwick), Berkeley Club, and Old England. The short-lived London House line was added to part of the 1936 and 1937 lists; by the roughly 1939 catalogue only six names remained. Each line occupying its own rung in the list shows that these were not a single "second-quality" heap, but grades separated from one another. Some of the names were also registered separately in the United States: Englandaire and Mayfair in 1931, Friar in 1934, and the sandblasted Windsor in 1951.
Shape Number and Finish

In the catalogues of the 1920s, shapes were named after London districts, holiday towns, and well-known Englishmen. Once the same shape began to be produced across several lines, this naming scheme stopped working. In the mid-1930s catalogues each shape was given a number, and the lines were also distinguished by the leading digit of that number: 5 for His Royal Highness, 6 for Mayfair, 7 for Old England and Berkeley Club (and often Henley Club too), 9 for Friar, 10 for Pickwick; Royal Stuart's number carries no prefix. The finish name also depends on the line — according to records, Friar is russet, Henley Club is dark red, Pickwick is walnut-toned, while Old England began with a roughened bowl. Among finishes, hand-carved rustic texture was largely reserved for Four Dot; the firm's own sandblasting method was registered under the name Ruff-Root in 1960.
Distributor Name and Slogan

The name of the American distributor appearing in catalogues and advertisements is the most useful clue, since it narrows the field to a fairly tight range: Maurice Rapoport (1923-1926), Sasieni, London Ltd. (1926-1933), London House (1933-1940), John Hudson Moore (1940-1955), and Sasieni of London (1955-1979). Slogans narrow the range further still — the phrase "World's Premier Pipe" corresponds to the late 1920s and early 1930s, while "Royal Pipe of England" belongs to the late 1930s.
After the Family Era

The family era closed when the firm was sold in 1979; according to records, the buyers were a group of South African investors led by Ian Chase, who kept the Four Dot name going. The company passed to James Russell's firm in 1986. At this point the shank stamp shrank from three lines to two: the first line reads "Sasieni 4 Dot," the second the finish name. On estate examples, this is the marker most often relied on to separate the family era from what came after.

r.x: The
Dunhill dating guide

describes a second way to convert the wording on a Dunhill pipe's shank into a production year. The method based on reading the patent number is covered in a separate entry; the path described here looks instead at three separate layers: the pipe's finish name, any special series stamp, and the small year suffix struck around the word ENGLAND. When these three pieces of information are set against each other, most pipes settle into a single year, or at worst a range of a few years.
What a Finish Tells You Is After

Whatever finish a pipe carries, it cannot be dated earlier than the year that finish came to market; this is the guide's roughest but most reliable sieve. At the head of the sequence is the smooth-polished Bruyere, which arrived with the start of briar production in 1910; this finish carried the letter "A," marking the top grade, on its shank up to 1975. Shell, the first of the sandblasts, was added in 1917. Sources diverge between 1930 and 1931 for Root, which brings out the grain; its shank stamp was long the letter "R." The light-brown sandblast Tanshell is mostly given as 1953, though some records show 1952. A similar hesitation surrounds the red Redbark, between 1972 and 1973; since examples stamped 1972 are known, the earlier date holds up better. Dark brown Cumberland, meanwhile, was introduced in 1980.

Two details outside the finish itself draw a similar boundary. The "Inner Tube" wording struck on the shank is not seen after 1934; the white dot on the mouthpiece, in most sources, is given a start date of 1915.
Special Series Stamps

Series names given in letters on the shank also narrow the period. The "H.W." stamp sets apart classically shaped bodies finished by hand; it is not found after the 1930s. The "D.R." stamp, struck on straight-grain bodies, matches the Bruyere finish up to 1929 and the Root finish afterward. Production of "O.D." pipes, made to the buyer's own design, ended between the late 1920s and early 1930s. Similar in name but not a continuation of it, ODA began in 1950 and ran to 1975; this series was not a commission but a standard, large-bowled production, and carried three-digit shape numbers beginning with 8. The Collector series, distinguished by bodies shaped by hand on a lathe from plateau briar, began in 1978.
Year Suffix and Shape Number

The reason the year code arose was a one-year defect guarantee given on the bowl: the firm needed to be able to tell when a given pipe was made. The real year information sits in the small digit right after the ENGLAND wording, or the patent number. For 1926–1934, a one- or two-digit number was used: 6 (1926), 7 (1927), 8 (1928), 9 (1929), 0 (1930), then 11 through 14 for 1931–1934. In these years the digit is seen falling sometimes after the patent number, sometimes after ENGLAND. In 1951 the group number indicating the pipe's length was added for the first time; that same year's suffix is the digit 1. In 1952 the shank wording began carrying the finish name instead of LONDON. The patent number is not found on the shank from 1955 onward. The underline beneath the digit was dropped in 1961; between 1965 and 1970 the digit grew to match the height of the "D" in ENGLAND, and between 1971 and 1975 it became two digits.

Shape numbers also give a date. In 1976–1977 the group number and finish code were dropped and the old shape numbers retired; in these two years three-, four-, and five-digit numbers are seen together. From 1978 onward all shape numbers moved to five digits, and the two-digit year suffix again became smaller than the "D" in ENGLAND.
Limits of the Guide

This system was never fully standardized at any point. The firm used different stamps depending on the export market, some of them in force for only a few months. Pipes with an incomplete or wrongly struck stamp are also not few. For this reason, rather than trusting a single mark, the finish, series stamp, year suffix, and shape number are read together; when two marks disagree, the result is given not as a single year but as a range.

r.x: Caminetto

is a pipe brand founded in 1968 in the northern Italian village of Cucciago, recognized by the mustache emblem inlaid on its mouthpiece. Because both the manufacturing arrangement and the stamping style changed between its first period, a little over a decade long, and its second period, which began again in the mid-1980s, the brand is treated as a separate dating topic among collectors.
The Partnership and the Brand Name

At the brand's core are two makers and a merchant. Giuseppe Ascorti, known in the circle as "Peppino," had worked more than a decade at the Castello workshop in Cantù, where he learned to work briar. His next-door neighbor in Cucciago, Luigi Radice, had also been making pipes at Castello since 1960. The two left the workshop at the end of 1968 and set up their own bench in Cucciago. The third partner was Gianni Davoli, who ran a tobacconist's shop in Milan; thanks to his wholesale contacts in America, sales and distribution fell to him.

The brand's name is the diminutive of the Italian word "camino," meaning fireplace. In time the partners themselves came to be called "i tre camini" — the three chimneys. Ascorti's and Radice's thick mustaches are the source both of the emblem inlaid on the mouthpiece and of the phrase associated with the brand, "la pipa del baffo" (the mustache pipe).
Growth and Break-up

Records say American distribution ran through the Tinder Box chain, and the rusticated Business line became the brand's best-known series. As demand grew, Davoli invested in machinery and his share in the company grew; reportedly annual production reached a few thousand pieces. The tension between series production tied to standard shape numbers and an approach based on handwork ended the partnership: Radice left in December 1979 and founded a brand under his own name in 1980. The Ascorti family also left the company that same year; after briefly producing under the name Sergio, they moved to production under their own surname. The Caminetto name was revived by Peppino's son, Roberto Ascorti; production in the new period is taken to have begun in 1986.
First-Period Stamps
In the first period the brand name is struck in two forms: script "Caminetto" or block letters in quotation marks. The location stamp, in turn, appears in three arrangements:
ASCORTI / RADICE / CUCCIAGO / CANTU-ITALY
HAND MADE IN ITALY / CUCCIAGO (Co)
MADE IN ITALY / CUCCIAGO (CANTU)

The first, carrying both makers' names, is taken as the earliest arrangement. The other two name the same place, since Cucciago is a locality within Cantù; for this reason the difference between them is not, by itself, a reliable dating guide. The shape of the mustache emblem on the mouthpiece is a more useful clue: pipes from roughly 1968–1975 carry a mustache resembling a bird in flight, while later years used one that resembles a double comma. Either can appear in gold or white. Some shanks also carry the Tinder Box's own crest.

Business-series pipes are stamped with the series name and shape number; the large size (king size) indicated by the KS that follows is generally accepted. The premium smooth and specialty-finish models, though collectors call them Prestige, do not carry that word on the shank; instead, model names such as Bagdad, Damasco, Excellence, Green Briar, Moustache, New Dear, Red Briar, Sable d'Or, and Torch are struck there.
Second-Period Numbering

After 1986, the stamping settled into a readable system. In the new period's first stamp format, a four-digit cluster stands next to the script Caminetto name: in order, shape, finish, series, and year of manufacture. In the format used later, the cluster shrinks to three — finish, a letter that is mostly "L" (though "R" or "B" appears on some shanks), and year. The finish digit reads as follows: 0 standard smooth, 1 natural straight grain, 2 natural smooth, 6 sandblast, 7 New Dear, 8 Business. Thanks to the year digit, the manufacture year of new-period pipes can be read directly on estate examples. On first-period pipes, dating at the level of a single year is not possible; only the ranges given by the stamp arrangement and the emblem's shape remain.

r.x: Dating English tinned tobacco

is the work of determining how old a tin of pipe tobacco packed in Britain is, drawing on the tin itself and its wording. Tins carry no production date; the collector narrows the range by stacking indirect clues that reinforce one another. The most widely used compilation of these clues is the work John C. Loring published in 1999.
Why Age Is Asked

A tin's age answers two separate questions at once. The first is maturity: in the English blend tradition, since the use of additives is kept narrow, flavor depends heavily on the leaf's own chemistry; high-sugar Virginia and Oriental leaves keep changing for decades inside a sealed tin, so tobacco aging is here directly a matter of taste. The second is identity. A blend carrying the same label may, depending on the year it was tinned, have come from a completely different firm, even a different country: the English tobacco industry began consolidating from the 1970s onward, and by the 1990s production of most blends had shifted to continental Europe. A similar threshold is recounted on the raw-material side; Syria is said to have restricted the use of curing wood in the 1970s to protect its forests, which withdrew Syrian latakia from the market.
Marks That Set a Firm Threshold on Their Own
Some marks push a tin firmly before or after a given year. The large

letter on the label is a lower bound: this mark was defined by Council Directive 76/211/EEC of 20 January 1976, and the United Kingdom brought its average-quantity rule into law with the Weights and Measures Act 1979. A tin carrying the ℮ mark, therefore, cannot be dated earlier than the late 1970s. The reverse doesn't hold; unmarked tins were also printed in the 1980s and 1990s.

The US federal tax stamp, or its remnant, found on tins that went to America sets an upper bound: these stamps were not used after mid-1959. The 1926 read on the stamp is the year of the law the tax rests on, not the tin's; what gives the date is the serial number. Stamp catalogues place series no. 102 in the early 1930s and series no. 125 in the mid-1950s; Loring's own rule of adding 29 to the series number arrives at roughly the same result. If the tin carries an importer's address, a third threshold arises: if the address shows an old-style postal zone number instead of a ZIP code, the tin falls before the ZIP system began on 1 July 1963.
Clues That Give a Rough Range

The tin's opening mechanism gives only a decade-scale range. The "knife lid" type has a thin, single-use inner lid and a loose outer lid meant to be cut open to access it; this type is accepted as dominant from the First World War through the 1960s, and the fixed-tab form of the outer lid was dropped in the early 1950s. The coin-twisted "coin twist" spread after the Second World War and had become the leading type by the 1970s. The ring-pull "pop top" arrived in the 1970s; that the opening instructions on the lid are given in words rather than only a diagram is taken as pointing to an earlier date than one with a diagram alone. The key-wound "key top" and the airtight-lidless "canister" are rarely seen on English tobaccos.

Label wording works at the same rough scale. The origin line reads mostly as "Great Britain," "England," "Scotland," or "Northern Ireland" before the 1980s, while "United Kingdom" comes to the fore with the 1980s. The weight unit moves in the same direction: tins showing only ounces point to the mid-1970s and earlier, tins showing ounces and grams together to the late 1970s and after, and tins showing only grams point, by weight alone, to after 1980.
Brand Turning Points

Individual brands also have fixed break years. For Dunhill tobaccos, this year is 1981: production of most blends passed that year to Murray, Sons & Co. in Belfast, and the origin line on the tins turned to "United Kingdom." For Rattray's, it is known that once the Perth shop closed around 1980, the blends were transferred to Robert McConnell. Handwritten dates on a tin should be treated with caution; they most often show not the manufacture year but the year the tin changed hands, or a previous owner's guess.

r.x: "Memories of Charatan Pipes and Notes on their Dating"
is an article published in 1998 in
The Pipe Collector

, the bulletin of the North American Society of Pipe Collectors (NASPC), that attempts to work out an approximate production date for Charatan pipes from their stamps and stem shapes. Its author, Ivy Ryan, was a pipe smoker who visited the Charatan workshop in London repeatedly from the mid-1960s to the early 1970s; the text draws not on factory records but on memories from those visits and on pipes that passed through the author's hands. It is one of the most frequently cited texts in dating Charatan pipes — and, just as often, one of the most disputed.
The Brand History the Article Relies On

The facts that frame the text are these: Charatan was founded in London by Frederick Charatan, reportedly in 1863; his son Reuben took over the business after his father's retirement, around 1910; and the workshop operated for many years on Prescot Street. The firm's departure from family ownership is dated to the early 1960s: the American importer Lane Limited bought the brand. Sources do not fully agree on either the founding year or the year of the sale; some compilations place the founding in the 1870s and the Lane takeover in 1962-1963. For this reason, both dates should be read as approximate rather than exact.

Later milestones are less disputed. Charatan bought the machinery of the Ben Wade workshop, which closed in 1965, though it never used those machines on Prescot Street. In the late 1970s, Lane Limited came under the Dunhill umbrella; the Prescot Street workshop closed in 1982, and production moved to another Dunhill facility. The brand name's move from Dunhill to J. B. Russell is dated to around 1988; some compilations place the new owner's production in the early 1990s.

r.x: The same article notes that the Double Comfort stem came into use in 1960, and that the "X" mark next to the shape number distinguishes pipes made with an ordinary saddle stem. It also gives a hierarchy of quality grades running from Belvedere up to Supreme, and states that new top grades were added to this hierarchy after 1965. For the general logic of stamp reading, see the pipe stamps and logos entry.
Why It Should Be Read with Caution

When republishing the text, Pipedia added a warning up front: a portion of Charatan collectors find some of the dating information incorrect or misleading. The author herself says she never had access to factory records, and that she was told the pre-war documents had been destroyed in the bombing. The sections of the text dealing with manufacturing methods and briar curing practices are observational accounts; they have not been confirmed by independent records. For this reason the article should be used not as a standalone dating authority, but as a testimony to be weighed against other sources.
